question:
Patient note:
A 34-year-old woman who designs user-interface graphics for a video-game studio was seen late this afternoon in the multidisciplinary rheumatology-medicine clinic at the request of her primary physician for a global status review before she resumes an international travel schedule that will take her to multiple game-developer conferences over the next year. At age 26 she developed symmetric polyarthritis of the metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints, recurrent oral ulcers, photosensitive malar erythema, and a persistently positive antinuclear antibody with high-titer double-stranded DNA antibodies; hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and low-dose prednisone were started at that time with good symptomatic control. Four years ago mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily replaced prednisone after she sought to minimize long-term glucocorticoid exposure, and she remains flare-free for the last 18 months, able to type eight-hour stretches during software “crunch” periods without morning stiffness or joint swelling. Endocrine surveillance two years ago uncovered fasting plasma glucose readings between 140 and 160 mg/dL on two occasions; hemoglobin A1c was 7.8 %, and she was started on metformin 1 g twice daily augmented by lifestyle coaching through a smartphone application. Her most recent A1c, drawn last week, was 6.9 %, finger-stick logs average 105–155 mg/dL before breakfast, and she denies visual blurring, paresthesias, claudication, nephropathy screening is negative for microalbuminuria, and retinal photography at the optometrist six months ago reported no hemorrhages or exudates. Serial comprehensive metabolic panels have for the past three years shown mild aminotransferase elevations—alanine aminotransferase ranging 52–68 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 44–60 U/L—with a homogeneous, slightly echogenic liver on ultrasound consistent with non-alcoholic fatty infiltration. There has been no jaundice, abdominal distension, hematemesis, or melena; total bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and the international normalized ratio 1.0, and abdominal Doppler imaging last month demonstrated patent portal and hepatic veins with no splenomegaly. She jogs three miles on an indoor track twice weekly, climbs three flights of stairs to her office without pausing, and has never used inhalers, been treated for bronchitis, or required antibiotics for winter “chest colds.” A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded during an employee health fair last year displayed normal sinus rhythm at 78 beats/min, no Q waves, and no ST-segment deviation, and a screening transthoracic echocardiogram performed by cardiology after she completed a charity 10-k run revealed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 64 % with normal chamber dimensions and no valvular abnormality. She has never felt crushing substernal pain, orthopnea, lower-extremity edema, sudden unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, or visual loss. Renal indices today show sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 112 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis is bland. Lipid panel last month revealed total cholesterol 182 mg/dL, LDL 108 mg/dL, HDL 54 mg/dL, and triglycerides 118 mg/dL; she takes rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly without myalgias. She quit smoking during college after accumulating 5 pack-years, drinks a glass of red wine with weekend dinners, and denies illicit drug use. Both parents are alive in their sixties—her mother has hypothyroidism, her father hypertension—but there is no family history of premature coronary disease, cerebrovascular accident, cirrhosis, or dementia. She herself has never been diagnosed with a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, stomach ulcers, cancer, or lymphoma, nor has she ever experienced weakness of one side of the body. She has no chronic lung conditions such as asthma or emphysema. Current medications include hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, metformin, rosuvastatin, cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily, and levonorgestrel–ethinyl estradiol oral contraceptive pills for cycle regulation; she takes ibuprofen sparingly for menstrual cramps and reports no drug allergies. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest discomfort, abdominal pain, early satiety, pruritus, hematochezia, dysuria, or rash beyond occasional photosensitive macules in midsummer. On examination she appears younger than her stated age, converses easily, and is oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg seated in the right arm, pulse 80 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, weight 70 kg, height 170 cm, body-mass index 24 kg/m². Sclerae are anicteric, oral mucosa shows two shallow healed aphthous scars, neck is supple with no lymphadenopathy or thyromegaly, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation is 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 °. The point of maximal impulse is localized to the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation with full excursion and no adventitious sounds. Abdomen is flat, nondistended, with normal bowel sounds; percussion is tympanitic, liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, smooth and non-tender, no splenic tip is felt, and there is no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Extremities are warm, nailfold capillaries exhibit no telangiectasias, radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and there is no edema. Neurologic examination reveals intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, negative Babinski bilaterally, and smooth tandem gait. Musculoskeletal inspection shows mild ulnar deviation at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints but no active synovitis, swelling, or tenderness; full wrist extension is preserved, and handgrip dynamometry measures 32 kg on the right and 30 kg on the left. Point-of-care capillary glucose just prior to examination is 138 mg/dL. A repeat electrocardiogram obtained today mirrors the prior tracing. She requests guidance on balancing antimalarial therapy during long-haul flights, timing of liver enzyme monitoring while traveling, safe immunization scheduling before departure, and strategies to maintain glycemic control when sampling regional cuisine abroad.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted comorbidities present at assessment.
- Age 34 (under 50): 0 points.
- Connective tissue disease: 1 point for systemic lupus erythematosus, even though treatment has controlled the arthritis and rash.
- Diabetes without end-organ damage: 1 point. She takes metformin and has no documented retinal, renal, or neurologic complication.
- Mild chronic liver disease: 1 point for fatty liver with persistent aminotransferase elevation. Preserved synthetic function and no evidence of portal hypertension argue against a higher severity category.
- Other qualifying comorbidities: 0 points.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
